terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: Scores quality as perception minus expectation on paired 22-item scales across five dimensions -- reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness -- so a dimension scoring 0 means expectations were met exactly and every negative number is a measured shortfall to fix.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how you would measure service quality is scored on the subtraction: measuring satisfaction alone cannot tell an over-promise from an under-delivery.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: Forecasts a new brand's settled share as cumulative penetration × repeat-purchase rate × buying-rate index — 40% × 25% × 1.2 = 12% share — so a launch that everybody tries and nobody buys twice collapses on the middle term no matter how large the trial figure looks in the panel data.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product forecast items give the three panel figures and expect the multiplied share; in a plan presentation the same arithmetic is what separates a trial problem, which advertising can fix, from a repeat problem, which only the product can.

terms.definition: A randomly selected slice of the target deliberately shown no advertising, so campaign lift is the exposed group's conversion rate minus the withheld group's — if exposed converts at 3.2% and the holdout at 2.6%, only 0.6 points were caused by the campaign and the rest would have happened anyway.
terms.whyItMatters: A client convinced a campaign drove every sale in its window is the setup for this method, and a competitor who can propose withholding a control group is answering a measurement question that platform-reported totals cannot.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Sells the finished product with its full marketing plan in a few representative cities while matched control cities keep the old plan, so the result read is the difference between the two areas rather than the test area's raw sales; the cost is secrecy, since rivals see the plan months early.
terms.whyItMatters: Launch roleplays ask how you would prove the plan works before national rollout; the matched control is the detail that turns a demo into a measurement.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: Multiplies target households × awareness % × trial % × availability (%ACV) × repeat % × units bought per repeat buyer to reach a first-year volume, so a chain of five decimals well below 1.0 shrinks 10,000,000 households into a few hundred thousand units, and each factor names a different budget line that has to be funded to move it.
terms.whyItMatters: Concept-test forecast questions supply the five percentages and expect the unit answer; walking the chain aloud is also how a plan defends why awareness money and distribution money are not substitutes for each other.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: Locates a failure in one of five gaps -- not knowing what customers expect, setting wrong standards, delivery that misses those standards, promotion promising what operations cannot deliver, and the customer gap between expectation and perception, which is produced by the first four.
terms.whyItMatters: Guest-recovery roleplays are scored on diagnosing which gap caused the complaint, since an over-promising ad and an untrained server call for opposite fixes.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: Paid media spend divided by net sales, times 100, then benchmarked against the category norm — a 3% ratio in a category averaging 8% flags underinvestment. It counts media only, so it always reads lower than the marketing expense ratio for the same plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review questions supply a company ratio and an industry average and ask whether spending is adequate; the comparison, not the raw number, is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Total spend divided by clicks received — $800 over 3,200 clicks is $0.25 — a pricing basis that charges only when someone acts, unlike cost per thousand, which charges for the impression whether or not anyone ever clicks it.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay asks which pricing model protects a small client's budget; the answer turns on whether the goal is awareness, where impressions are the product, or traffic, where only the click is worth paying for.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: Something buyers do not think to look for and may not know exists, so it has to be sold to them rather than bought -- burial plots, life insurance, a brand-new category's first entrant; a specialty good is the opposite pole, actively hunted by name with special effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling roleplays for insurance or services are scored on recognizing that no one walks in asking, which forces prospecting and personal selling rather than displays.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: Sets the average category buyer's annual purchase volume at 1.00 and states a brand's buyers against it, so 1.30 means the people who choose this brand buy 30% more of the category per year than the typical buyer; it is the third multiplier that converts a penetration figure and a repeat rate into a share estimate.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the factor students silently drop from a share forecast, turning a 12% answer into 10%, and it is the evidence behind a plan that argues for targeting heavy users instead of chasing more triers.

terms.definition: Opens divided by messages delivered — not messages sent — so 4,000 opens on 20,000 delivered is 20% while the same 4,000 against 25,000 sent looks like 16%. The count only fires when a tracking pixel loads, so image blocking and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection both distort it.
terms.whyItMatters: A direct-marketing roleplay reporting a suspiciously high figure after a privacy change is testing whether the competitor knows the metric is inferred from a pixel and will point to clicks as the reliable measure instead.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: The band between desired service, what the customer hopes for, and adequate service, the least they will accept: performance inside the band passes unnoticed, above it delights, below it triggers complaint or defection, and the band narrows sharply in urgent or first-time-fix situations.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about exceeding guest expectations are scored on knowing that ordinary delivery earns nothing; the band explains why effort spent in the middle is invisible.

terms.definition: Three decisions taken strictly in order — segment the market on one chosen base, target the segments worth serving against a stated attractiveness test, then position the offer against a named competitive set — where each step's output constrains the next; a positioning claim written before the segment is chosen has nobody in particular to be different for, which is why reordering the letters produces a plan that cannot be defended.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan roleplays are graded on sequence as much as content; presenting a promotion idea before naming the segment invites the judge to ask who it is for.

terms.definition: Total marketing spend divided by net sales, times 100 — programs, salaries, agency fees and campaigns, not just media — so it answers what the plan costs to run. Marketing ROI asks the opposite question, what the same spend returned.
terms.whyItMatters: Control questions ask which metric shows a plan is over budget versus which shows it was unprofitable; naming the wrong one loses the item even when the arithmetic is right.

terms.definition: Copies a publication actually distributes in an average issue, audited by the Alliance for Audited Media, as opposed to readership, which multiplies those copies by a pass-along factor of roughly 2 to 3 — so a 500,000-copy magazine can legitimately claim 1,200,000 readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Print-buying items give one vehicle's audited copies and a rival's claimed readers and ask which is the larger audience; the competitor has to convert both to the same basis before the cost-per-thousand comparison means anything.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: A tangible item expected to survive repeated use, the standard statistical cutoff being an expected life of three years or more, which is why appliances and vehicles qualify; nondurables are consumed in one or a few uses and are bought on habit rather than deliberation.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty, financing, and personal-selling effort all follow this split, so an exam item on why one product gets a service plan and another does not is answered with the three-year line.

terms.definition: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging — the contour of a Coca-Cola bottle, a restaurant chain's interior scheme — protected under Lanham Act section 43(a) only when it is non-functional and has acquired secondary meaning in buyers' minds; product design trade dress can never be inherently distinctive, so unlike a coined word mark it always requires evidence that consumers link the look to a single source.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a competitor copying a store's look are scored on naming this protection and its two conditions; calling it a trademark or a copyright is the common miss.

terms.definition: Scales a controlled market's result to a national number by dividing the test volume by that market's share of national category volume — 60,000 units in a market holding 2% of national volume projects to 3,000,000 units — then discounting for support levels, distribution or pricing that cannot be repeated nationwide.
terms.whyItMatters: Rollout questions give the test units plus the market's percentage of national volume and expect the projection; the discount step is what a judge presses on when a plan's national number looks suspiciously clean.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: The severest federal recall classification, used when a defect carries a reasonable probability of serious injury or death; Class II covers defects whose harm is temporary or medically reversible and where serious harm is remote, and Class III covers violations unlikely to cause any harm.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-protection questions give a defect scenario and ask how urgently the firm must act; the class decides the notification reach and the speed regulators expect.

terms.definition: Incremental gross profit from a campaign minus its marketing cost, divided by that marketing cost: $150,000 of incremental revenue at a 40% gross margin against $30,000 of spend is ($60,000 - $30,000) / $30,000, or 100%. It runs on margin rather than revenue, and only on the lift a holdout group shows the campaign actually caused, so a campaign whose sales would have happened anyway returns a negative figure no matter how large the revenue number looks.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks whether a promotion paid for itself, the graded answer is this ratio on margin with a baseline, not the raw sales the campaign period produced.

terms.definition: Averages the size of forecast misses ignoring their direction — the sum of |actual − forecast| ÷ the number of periods — which keeps the error in the product's own units instead of percentages, and roughly 1.25 times this figure approximates one standard deviation of forecast error for setting a buffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-error items hand six periods of actuals and forecasts and expect this average computed; it is also the denominator of the tracking signal, so an error here quietly breaks the control check built on top of it.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: The Consumer Product Safety Act duty to notify the Commission within 24 hours of obtaining information that a product contains a defect creating a substantial hazard, fails a mandatory standard, or poses an unreasonable risk -- and the duty applies even when the firm still disputes the defect.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and consumer-protection roleplays test whether you report before finishing your own investigation; waiting for certainty is the answer that loses the indicator and, in practice, draws the fine.

terms.definition: Merchandise sold under the retailer's own name and sourced from a contract manufacturer, typically carrying a retail gross margin about 10 percentage points above the comparable national brand — roughly 35% against 25% — while retailing 15% to 30% cheaper, because the retailer carries no national advertising cost; the national brand by contrast is owned, advertised and priced by the manufacturer, who keeps that margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about shelf space are settled with this margin arithmetic, and a competitor who argues only that the store brand is cheaper has missed why the retailer prefers it.

terms.definition: (actual minus planned) / planned x 100, carried on every line of the marketing plan: $92,000 delivered against a $100,000 forecast is -8%. The sign alone does not say good or bad — negative on revenue is unfavorable, negative on expense is favorable.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-year review items give planned and actual columns and ask which lines need action; competitors who read every negative as a problem flag the underspent line that is actually helping.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Nothing can be inspected, weighed, or returned before purchase, so buyers judge search qualities beforehand, experience qualities only during delivery, and credence qualities -- a surgeon's technique, a tax opinion -- never at all; a good lets buyers verify most attributes before paying.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay contrasting service marketing with product marketing is scored on the tangible cues you add -- uniforms, facilities, guarantees -- to stand in for inspection.

terms.definition: The sum of the discounted lifetime values of a firm's current and future customers — the asset value of the customer base itself — which can rise while brand equity falls, as when a firm buys volume with deep discounts and wins customers who think less of the name each year; brand equity is the value held in what buyers believe about the mark, customer equity the value held in the relationships and their future cash.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a discount-driven growth plan is healthy, the judged answer separates the two equities and says which one the plan is spending down.

terms.definition: Divides the running cumulative forecast error by the mean absolute deviation to test whether misses are random noise or one-sided drift; a value wandering past ±4 says the model is systematically off and must be re-fit rather than nudged, while a value oscillating around zero says the error is noise and the model should be left alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-control questions supply a cumulative error and a MAD and want both the ratio and the keep-or-refit call against the limit, not a general remark that the forecast looks wrong.

terms.definition: Replacement time or space a medium owes when a commitment ran in the wrong position, ran late, or fell short of guaranteed delivery — a station that guarantees 150 gross rating points and delivers 120 owes those 30 points back as inventory, not as a cash refund.
terms.whyItMatters: An under-delivery roleplay tests whether the competitor asks for the right remedy; demanding money back where the contract promises replacement inventory usually forfeits the claim entirely.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: A label a written warranty may carry only if it repairs defects free within a reasonable time, puts no duty on the buyer beyond giving notice, does not limit the duration of implied warranties, and offers a refund or replacement after a reasonable number of failed repairs; missing any one forces the 'limited' label.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty roleplays ask what a store may print on the tag; a written warranty that charges a handling fee cannot be called full, and knowing which of the four conditions broke is the scoring point.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: Scores every step of a forecasting process by the accuracy points it adds over the naive baseline — baseline MAPE 20%, statistical model 17%, sales-team override 19% — so the model step is worth +3 points and the override is worth −2 and should be removed from the process rather than coached.
terms.whyItMatters: Process-improvement items ask which forecasting step to cut, and the negative-value step is the answer; it is also the numeric way a plan review argues that field overrides are hurting the number instead of helping it.

terms.definition: The FTC doctrine that an advertiser must already hold the evidence for an objective claim before that claim runs, and that health or performance claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence — the line separating a provable assertion from puffery, which makes no measurable claim and needs no proof.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants to advertise that a product works twice as fast is asking a legal question, and the competitor is scored on requiring the proof up front rather than promising to find it if challenged.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: The geographic zone a location actually draws customers from, mapped as rings: the primary ring supplies roughly 60-75% of customers, the secondary another 15-25%, and the fringe the scattered remainder. It sets the population a site's forecast is allowed to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and retail-expansion cases give customer ZIP-code counts and ask how far the draw reaches; forecasting against the whole metropolitan population instead of the primary ring inflates every downstream number.

terms.definition: Coverage, mentions and shares a brand receives without buying placement — as against paid media, which is bought inventory the brand controls outright, and owned media, which is the brand's own site, list and channels. Only the paid third can be guaranteed to appear on a chosen date.
terms.whyItMatters: A launch-planning roleplay that leans on press pickup for a fixed launch day is the trap this term defends against, and public-relations items on the exam expect the three-way split to be named, not just the unpaid half.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: Ehrenberg's empirical finding that a brand with a smaller customer base is punished twice over — fewer people buy it at all, and those who do buy it less often — so measured loyalty is almost entirely a consequence of penetration rather than an independent lever; the practical consequence is that a small brand's plan to grow purely by deepening loyalty among existing buyers contradicts the pattern found in essentially every category studied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a retention-only growth plan for a small brand is a trap; naming this regularity and redirecting toward penetration is the scored move.

terms.definition: Divides the standard deviation of period demand by its mean to grade how forecastable a series is: under about 0.25 a single point forecast is dependable, and above roughly 0.50 the item is erratic enough that the plan must carry a range and a buffer instead of one number.
terms.whyItMatters: Planning questions ask which item deserves a statistical forecast and which needs judgment plus safety stock; the ratio decides it, and the threshold is the part of the item being tested.

terms.definition: The share of a rebate offer's buyers who qualify but never file the paperwork, which is why a $50 mail-in rebate with 40% of buyers never claiming actually costs the manufacturer $30 per unit sold — the gap between a promotion's face value and its real cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing-and-promotion roleplay comparing an instant discount against a mail-in offer of the same face value turns on this: the two look identical to the customer and cost the manufacturer very different amounts.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: A comprehensive, systematic, independent and periodic examination of a firm's whole marketing environment, objectives, strategies and activities — all four adjectives are required, so a review of one campaign conducted by the team that ran it qualifies as none of them; its deliverable is a ranked list of corrective actions, not a score or a performance rating.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how you would diagnose a marketing department that is missing its targets, the independence and scope conditions are what distinguish an audit from an internal post-mortem.

terms.definition: Personal income for an area minus personal tax payments — the disposable dollars residents can actually spend, not gross earnings. It is the income term inside a buying power index, which weights it against the area's population and retail sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Territory and market-selection items give gross income for two cities and expect the after-tax spendable figure to drive the ranking, because a high-tax market supports less spending than its wage level suggests.

terms.definition: Paid placement built to match the form and feel of the surrounding editorial content, which the FTC requires be labeled Ad, Sponsored or Paid before the reader clicks — precisely because matching the publisher's format is what stops a reader from telling it apart from unpaid editorial.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay proposing an article that reads like the site's own reporting is scored on whether the competitor puts the disclosure ahead of the click, and exam items contrast it with publicity, which is unpaid and carries no label duty.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.
